problems.title: Count the rows
problems.statement_md: A cafe wants to know how busy it has been. Return one row with one column, `order_count`, holding the number of orders in the table.

tables.name: cafe_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. `tip` is NULL when the customer left no tip.

hints_md: Which aggregate function counts how many rows there are?
Some `tip` values are NULL. Is that a reason to leave any order out of the count?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** an aggregate function squeezes many rows into one value.

**Shape:** no grouping, no filter. The whole table collapses into a single row.

**Syntax:** `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` counts only the rows where that column is not NULL.

**Watch out:** counting a column that contains NULLs silently skips those rows.

solutions.label: COUNT(*)
solutions.explain_md: `COUNT(*)` counts every row, whatever the values are.
solutions.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM cafe_orders;

solutions.label: COUNT of a column without NULLs
solutions.explain_md: `order_id` is never NULL, so counting it gives the same number as counting rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT COUNT(order_id) AS order_count
FROM cafe_orders;

traps.explain_md: `COUNT(tip)` only counts orders that have a tip. The orders with a NULL tip are skipped, so the answer is too small.
traps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(tip) AS order_count
FROM cafe_orders;

problems.title: COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column)
problems.statement_md: A library keeps a record of every loan. A loan that has not come back yet has a NULL `returned_on`. Return one row with `total_loans` (all loans) and `returned_loans` (loans that have been returned).

tables.name: loans
tables.description_md: One row per loan. `returned_on` is NULL while the book is still out.

hints_md: One of the two numbers should count every row, the other only rows where a column has a value.
Which form of `COUNT` ignores NULLs?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(column)` are different questions: how many rows, versus how many non-NULL values.

**Shape:** one table, no grouping, two aggregates side by side in one row.

**Syntax:** `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(some_column)`.

**Watch out:** if a column has no NULLs at all the two forms agree, which hides the difference until real data arrives.

solutions.label: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)
solutions.explain_md: `COUNT(*)` counts all loans; `COUNT(returned_on)` skips the NULLs, leaving only returned loans.

solutions.label: SUM of a yes/no test
solutions.explain_md: A CASE expression gives 1 for a returned loan and 0 otherwise; adding them up counts the returned ones.

traps.explain_md: `COUNT(returned_on)` is used for both columns, so `total_loans` only counts returned loans.
`COUNT(*)` is used for both columns, so `returned_loans` is just the total again.

problems.title: How many different customers
problems.statement_md: A bookshop wants to know how many different customers have bought something. Return one row with one column, `customer_count`. A customer who bought several times counts once.

tables.name: bookshop_sales
tables.description_md: One row per purchase. The same `customer_id` can appear many times.

hints_md: Counting rows would count a repeat customer every time they appear. How can you ask `COUNT` to ignore repeats?
Look for a keyword you can put inside the brackets.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** counting unique values rather than rows.

**Shape:** no grouping; one aggregate over a single column, with duplicates removed before counting.

**Syntax:** `COUNT(DISTINCT column)`.

**Watch out:** `COUNT(column)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` only differ when values repeat, so test on data that does repeat.

solutions.label: COUNT(DISTINCT)
solutions.explain_md: `DISTINCT` inside `COUNT` removes repeated customer ids before counting.
solutions.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM bookshop_sales;

solutions.label: Count a list of distinct ids
solutions.explain_md: First build the list of unique customer ids, then count its rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM bookshop_sales) AS unique_customers;

traps.explain_md: `COUNT(customer_id)` counts purchases, not people, so repeat customers are counted every time.
traps.sql:
SELECT COUNT(customer_id) AS customer_count
FROM bookshop_sales;

problems.title: Total, average, smallest, largest
problems.statement_md: A garden centre wants a quick summary of its plant prices. Return one row with `total_value` (sum of all prices), `average_price` (rounded to 2 decimals), `cheapest` and `priciest`.

tables.name: plants
tables.description_md: One row per plant on sale.

hints_md: Four different aggregate functions are needed, each on the `price` column.
Which function rounds a number to a chosen number of decimals? Its second argument is the number of decimals.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** several aggregates can be calculated together in a single pass over the table.

**Shape:** one row out; each output column is its own aggregate. The rounding goes around the average.

**Syntax:** `SUM(col)`, `AVG(col)`, `MIN(col)`, `MAX(col)`, `ROUND(value, decimals)`.

**Watch out:** an average often has many decimals; round it only in the final output.

solutions.label: Four aggregates
solutions.explain_md: `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` all look at the whole table; `ROUND(..., 2)` trims the average.
solutions.sql:
SELECT SUM(price) AS total_value,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 2) AS average_price,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS priciest
FROM plants;

solutions.label: Average as sum divided by count
solutions.explain_md: The average is just the total divided by the number of plants.
solutions.sql:
SELECT SUM(price) AS total_value,
       ROUND(SUM(price) / COUNT(*), 2) AS average_price,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS priciest
FROM plants;

traps.explain_md: `ROUND(AVG(price), 1)` keeps only 1 decimal, but the question asks for 2.
traps.sql:
SELECT SUM(price) AS total_value,
       ROUND(AVG(price), 1) AS average_price,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS priciest
FROM plants;

traps.explain_md: `ROUND(AVG(price))` with no second argument rounds to a whole number.
traps.sql:
SELECT SUM(price) AS total_value,
       ROUND(AVG(price)) AS average_price,
       MIN(price) AS cheapest,
       MAX(price) AS priciest
FROM plants;

problems.title: Average ignores NULLs
problems.statement_md: A recipe site lets visitors leave a comment with or without a star rating; when no stars were given, `stars` is NULL. Return one row with `avg_stars`: the average star rating over the ratings that actually have stars, rounded to 2 decimals.

tables.name: recipe_ratings
tables.description_md: One row per visitor response. `stars` is 1 to 5, or NULL if the visitor only left a comment.

hints_md: Think about what `AVG` does with a NULL value in the column. Does it need your help?
If you replace NULL by a number before averaging, you change the denominator. Is a missing rating the same as a 0-star rating?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** aggregate functions other than `COUNT(*)` skip NULLs, which is usually what you want.

**Shape:** one table, no grouping, one aggregate, rounded at the end.

**Syntax:** `AVG(column)` averages the non-NULL values; `COALESCE(col, 0)` swaps NULL for 0.

**Watch out:** turning NULL into 0 before averaging pulls the average down, because the missing values now count as real zeros.

solutions.label: AVG skips NULLs
solutions.explain_md: `AVG` only looks at rows where `stars` has a value, so the missing ratings are left out of both the sum and the count.
solutions.sql:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(stars), 2) AS avg_stars
FROM recipe_ratings;

solutions.label: Filter the NULLs out first
solutions.explain_md: `WHERE` removes the rows without stars, then `AVG` averages what is left. Same answer, more explicit.

traps.explain_md: `COALESCE(stars, 0)` turns every missing rating into a 0-star rating, so those rows now count in the average and drag it down.
traps.sql:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(stars, 0)), 2) AS avg_stars
FROM recipe_ratings;

problems.title: Totals per group
problems.statement_md: A cinema wants to know which snack type earns the most. Return `product_type` and `total_amount` (the sum of `amount`) for each product type, highest total first, ties by `product_type`.

tables.name: concession_sales
tables.description_md: One row per snack sale at the cinema kiosk.

hints_md: You want one output row per product type. Which clause makes rows with the same value collapse into one group?
Every column in `SELECT` must either be in that clause or be inside an aggregate function.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `GROUP BY` splits the rows into buckets by a column, then each aggregate is calculated per bucket.

**Shape:** one row per distinct product type, with the sum of its amounts, sorted by that sum.

**Syntax:** `GROUP BY key` makes one group per key value; an aggregate in SELECT (`SUM`, `COUNT`, ...) is computed once per group.

**Watch out:** grouping by a unique column (like an id) makes every row its own group, so nothing is combined.

solutions.label: GROUP BY with SUM
solutions.explain_md: Rows are grouped by `product_type`; `SUM(amount)` adds up each group. The sort puts the largest total first, with the name as tie-break.
solutions.sql:
SELECT product_type, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM concession_sales
GROUP BY product_type
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, product_type;

traps.explain_md: Grouping by `sale_id` makes every sale its own group, so nothing is totalled per product type.
traps.sql:
SELECT product_type, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM concession_sales
GROUP BY sale_id, product_type
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, product_type;

problems.title: Count per group
problems.statement_md: A school wants to see how many students are in each class. Return `class_name` and `student_count`, largest class first, ties by `class_name`.

tables.name: students
tables.description_md: One row per student. `club` is NULL when the student has not joined a club.

hints_md: You want one row per class, so group by the class column.
Which form of `COUNT` counts rows no matter what the other columns contain?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** counting rows inside each group.

**Shape:** group by class, count the rows in each group, then sort by that count with the class name as tie-break.

**Syntax:** `GROUP BY key` makes one group per key value; an aggregate in SELECT is computed once per group. ORDER BY can sort by an aggregate.

**Watch out:** `COUNT(column)` skips NULLs in that column, so a group can look smaller than it really is.

solutions.label: COUNT(*) per class
solutions.explain_md: Each class forms a group; `COUNT(*)` counts its rows. Sorting by the count descending and then by name makes the order stable.
solutions.sql:
SELECT class_name, COUNT(*) AS student_count
FROM students
GROUP BY class_name
ORDER BY student_count DESC, class_name;

traps.explain_md: `COUNT(club)` skips students without a club, so the class sizes are wrong and the order changes.
traps.sql:
SELECT class_name, COUNT(club) AS student_count
FROM students
GROUP BY class_name
ORDER BY student_count DESC, class_name;

problems.title: Group by two columns
problems.statement_md: A bakery chain sells bread, cakes and pastry in two stores. Return `store`, `category` and `total_amount` (the sum of `amount`) for every store and category pair that has sales, ordered by `store` and then `category`.
hints_md: A group here is a combination: one store and one category together.
You can list more than one column after the grouping keyword, separated by commas.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a group can be defined by several columns at once; each distinct combination is one group.

**Shape:** one row per store and category pair, with a sum, sorted by both.

**Syntax:** `GROUP BY a, b`.

**Watch out:** every non-aggregate column in `SELECT` must also appear in `GROUP BY`; leaving one out loses that detail from the output.

solutions.label: GROUP BY store, category
solutions.explain_md: Each store and category pair is one group, and `SUM(amount)` totals its sales.
solutions.sql:
SELECT store, category, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM bakery_sales
GROUP BY store, category
ORDER BY store, category;

traps.explain_md: Grouping by store alone loses the category: the category breakdown is gone and you only get one total per store.
traps.sql:
SELECT store, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM bakery_sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;

problems.title: Only groups above a threshold
problems.statement_md: A delivery company wants to reward its busiest couriers. Return `courier` and `deliveries` (the number of deliveries) for couriers with more than 2 deliveries, most deliveries first, ties by `courier`.
hints_md: First count deliveries per courier. Then you need a condition on that count.
Which clause filters groups after they have been formed, the way `WHERE` filters individual rows?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `HAVING` is the filter for groups, applied after the aggregates are calculated.

**Shape:** group by courier, count, keep only groups whose count passes the test, then sort.

**Syntax:** `HAVING` filters groups after GROUP BY, and may use aggregates; `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and may not.

**Watch out:** "more than 2" and "at least 2" are different; check what happens to a group of exactly 2.

solutions.label: HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
solutions.explain_md: The rows are grouped per courier and counted; `HAVING` then drops the groups that did not pass the test.
solutions.sql:
SELECT courier, COUNT(*) AS deliveries
FROM deliveries
GROUP BY courier
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY deliveries DESC, courier;

traps.explain_md: `>= 2` lets in couriers with exactly 2 deliveries, but the question says more than 2.
traps.sql:
SELECT courier, COUNT(*) AS deliveries
FROM deliveries
GROUP BY courier
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY deliveries DESC, courier;

problems.title: WHERE before, HAVING after
problems.statement_md: A clinic wants to find doctors who earned more than 200 from appointments that were actually completed. Return `doctor` and `completed_total` (the sum of `fee` over completed appointments) for those doctors, highest total first, ties by `doctor`. Cancelled appointments must not count.

tables.name: appointments
tables.description_md: One row per booked appointment. `status` is `'completed'` or `'cancelled'`.

hints_md: There are two separate conditions: one about single rows (their status) and one about the group total. Which clause suits each?
Rows you do not want in a total should be removed before the total is calculated.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `WHERE` filters rows before grouping; `HAVING` filters groups after aggregating. Each condition belongs to the right stage.

**Shape:** first keep only the completed rows, then group per doctor and sum, then keep groups whose sum passes the test.

**Syntax:** `WHERE row_condition GROUP BY key HAVING aggregate_condition`.

**Watch out:** if the row filter is missing, the unwanted rows are still added into every total before `HAVING` looks at it.

solutions.label: WHERE then HAVING
solutions.explain_md: `WHERE` throws away cancelled appointments first, so they never reach the sum; `HAVING` then tests the total.
solutions.sql:
SELECT doctor, SUM(fee) AS completed_total
FROM appointments
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY doctor
HAVING SUM(fee) > 200
ORDER BY completed_total DESC, doctor;

solutions.label: Conditional sum inside HAVING
solutions.explain_md: No `WHERE`: a `CASE` adds the fee only when the appointment was completed, and `HAVING` tests that sum.
solutions.sql:
SELECT doctor,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN fee ELSE 0 END) AS completed_total
FROM appointments
GROUP BY doctor
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'completed' THEN fee ELSE 0 END) > 200
ORDER BY completed_total DESC, doctor;

traps.explain_md: With no row filter, cancelled appointments are added into each total, so Lee passes with fees that were never earned and the other totals are inflated.
traps.sql:
SELECT doctor, SUM(fee) AS completed_total
FROM appointments
GROUP BY doctor
HAVING SUM(fee) > 200
ORDER BY completed_total DESC, doctor;

problems.title: Groups with at least two different
problems.statement_md: A music app wants to find listeners who explore. Return `listener` and `artist_count` (the number of different artists they played) for listeners who played at least 2 different artists, highest `artist_count` first, ties by `listener`.

tables.name: plays
tables.description_md: One row per song played. The same listener can play the same artist many times.

hints_md: You are counting something different from rows here. What did you use in an earlier problem to count unique values?
You need that unique count both in the output and as the group filter.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** combine `COUNT(DISTINCT ...)` with `HAVING` to filter groups by how many different values they hold.

**Shape:** group per listener, count unique artists, keep groups with at least two, sort.

**Syntax:** `HAVING` filters groups after GROUP BY, and may use aggregates. `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts unique non-NULL values.

**Watch out:** a plain `COUNT(*)` counts repeated plays of the same artist, so one fan of one artist can look adventurous.

solutions.label: HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT)
solutions.explain_md: Per listener, `COUNT(DISTINCT artist)` ignores repeated plays of the same artist; `HAVING` keeps those with at least two.
solutions.sql:
SELECT listener, COUNT(DISTINCT artist) AS artist_count
FROM plays
GROUP BY listener
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT artist) >= 2
ORDER BY artist_count DESC, listener;

traps.explain_md: `COUNT(*)` counts plays, not artists, so Mia and Omar pass by replaying a single artist.
traps.sql:
SELECT listener, COUNT(*) AS artist_count
FROM plays
GROUP BY listener
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY artist_count DESC, listener;

problems.title: The biggest group
problems.statement_md: A gym wants to know which city most of its members live in. Return one row with `city` and `member_count` for the city with the most members. There is no tie for first place.
hints_md: First produce a member count per city. Then think about how to sort those counts so the largest is on top.
After sorting, how can you keep only the first row?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a group count can be sorted like any column, then trimmed to the top row.

**Shape:** group by city, count, order by the count with the biggest first, keep one row.

**Syntax:** ORDER BY can sort by an aggregate or its alias; `LIMIT n` keeps the top n rows.

**Watch out:** `ORDER BY` sorts ascending by default, so forgetting `DESC` returns the smallest group.

solutions.label: ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 1
solutions.explain_md: Group per city, sort the groups by their count from largest to smallest, and `LIMIT 1` keeps only the top group.
solutions.sql:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS member_count
FROM gym_members
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY member_count DESC, city
LIMIT 1;

traps.explain_md: Without `DESC` the sort starts at the smallest group, so the city with the fewest members is returned.
traps.sql:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS member_count
FROM gym_members
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY member_count, city
LIMIT 1;

traps.explain_md: Sorting by the city name instead of the count returns the alphabetically first city, which has nothing to do with size.
traps.sql:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS member_count
FROM gym_members
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY city
LIMIT 1;
